latency.def: How long one request takes, from start to finish, usually in milliseconds. Response time as the user sees it includes any waiting in queues.

throughput.def: How much work gets done per unit of time, like requests per second. A system can have high throughput and still be slow for each request.

percentile.def: The value below which that share of measurements falls. p95 is 327 milliseconds when 95 in 100 requests take 327 or less.

median.def: The middle value: half the requests are faster, half slower. Unlike the mean, a few very slow requests can't drag it up.

tail-latency.def: The slowest requests, measured by high percentiles like p99 or p99.9. Often the users who matter most: the biggest baskets, the most data.

tail-amplification.def: A request that waits for many backend calls is as slow as the slowest one, so rare slow calls become common slow pages.

queueing-delay.def: Time a request waits before any work starts. It grows steeply as a server nears 100 percent busy.

slo.def: Service level objective: a target stated as a percentile, like 95 percent of checkouts in under one second.

lines.hook.1: Some customers say the bakery's website feels slow. But the dashboard says the average page takes a hundred and seventy milliseconds.
lines.hook.2: Both are true. This lesson is about measuring speed honestly, the way interviewers expect you to.
lines.terms.1: Two different words first. Each dot is one request to the site.
lines.terms.2: How long one request takes, start to finish, is its <k>latency</k>.
lines.terms.3: How many requests finish each second is <k>throughput</k>.
lines.terms.4: They're not the same. A busy site can finish lots of requests per second, while each one still waits a long time.
lines.dist.1: Here are two hundred requests to the bakery's site, grouped by how long they took.
lines.dist.2: Most are quick, under about a hundred and twenty milliseconds. But a few take seconds. That long stretch on the right is the tail.

dist.3.caption: The average is 170 ms. Hardly any request actually takes that long.
dist.3.voice: The average is a hundred and seventy milliseconds. Hardly any request actually takes that long.

lines.dist.ask: Half the requests are faster than what?
lines.dist.mean: That's the average. A handful of very slow requests drags it up. The middle value is lower.
lines.dist.median: Right. The middle request: a hundred and one milliseconds.
lines.dist.fifty: Lower than most. The middle request takes a hundred and one milliseconds.
lines.dist.4: The middle value is the <k>median</k>, or p50. It's a <k>percentile</k>: half the requests are at or below it.

tail.1.caption: Now the slow end. The 95th percentile, p95, is 327 ms.
tail.1.voice: Now the slow end. The ninety-fifth percentile, p95, is three hundred and twenty-seven milliseconds.

tail.2.caption: And p99 is over 2 seconds. One request in a hundred waits more than two seconds.
tail.2.voice: And p99 is over two seconds. One request in a hundred waits more than two seconds.

lines.tail.3: That's <k id="tail-latency">tail latency</k>. And the slow requests are often the valuable ones: the biggest baskets, the loyal customers with the most history.
lines.tail.4: So report percentiles, not the average: p50 for the typical user, p95 and p99 for the unlucky ones.

p99.1.caption: Your turn. The table requests has one row per request, with its time in ms. Find the p99.
p99.1.voice: Your turn. The table requests has one row per request, with its time in milliseconds. Find the p99.

lines.p99.ask: There are two hundred rows, so p99 is the hundred and ninety-eighth fastest. Sort, skip, and take one.

p99.hint.caption: ORDER BY ms LIMIT 1 OFFSET 197: skip 197 rows, take the 198th.
p99.hint.voice: Order by the time, limit one, offset a hundred and ninety-seven. Skip a hundred and ninety-seven rows, and take the next.

lines.p99.error: The database couldn't run that. Read the message under the editor.
lines.p99.extra: Just one value, please: the p99.
lines.p99.missing: Not quite. Sort ascending, skip a hundred and ninety-seven, and take one.
lines.p99.done: Two thousand and ninety-three milliseconds. That's the number the unlucky customers feel.
lines.amp.1: It gets worse. To show the checkout page, the site calls several services: prices, stock, the basket, loyalty points.
lines.amp.2: The page can't finish until the slowest call does. So if any one call hits its slow tail, the whole page is slow.
lines.amp.ask: Each call is slow one time in a hundred. The page makes ten calls. How often is the page slow?
lines.amp.one: It's worse than that. Ten chances to be unlucky: about one page in ten.
lines.amp.ten: Right. About one in ten. Nearly ten percent.
lines.amp.half: Not quite that bad yet. About one page in ten, for ten calls.
lines.amp.3: With a hundred calls, nearly two pages in three are slow. That's <k id="tail-amplification">tail amplification</k>. It's why big systems obsess over p99.
lines.queue.1: One more source of slowness: waiting in line. A request can't start until the server is free.
lines.queue.2: At half busy, requests barely wait. At eighty percent, waits start to build.
lines.queue.3: At ninety-five percent busy, response time is four times what it was at eighty. The last bit of capacity is the most expensive.
lines.queue.4: That wait before any work starts is <k id="queueing-delay">queueing delay</k>. Throughput barely rises, while latency shoots up.
lines.checkout.1: Your turn again. The team promises: ninety-five percent of checkouts in under one second. Check it.
lines.checkout.ask: Find the p95 for the checkout endpoint. There are fifty checkout requests, so it's the forty-eighth fastest.

checkout.hint.caption: WHERE endpoint = '/checkout' ORDER BY ms LIMIT 1 OFFSET 47
checkout.hint.voice: Where the endpoint is checkout, order by the time, limit one, offset forty-seven.

lines.checkout.error: The database couldn't run that. Check the quotes around slash checkout.
lines.checkout.missing: Not quite. Only checkout requests, sorted, skip forty-seven, take one.
lines.checkout.done: Nine hundred and eighty-four milliseconds: the promise holds, just. A promise stated as a percentile is an <k>SLO</k>.

quiz.q1.caption: Average response time is 170 ms, but the median is 101 ms. What does that tell you?
quiz.q1.voice: Average response time is a hundred and seventy milliseconds, but the median is a hundred and one. What does that tell you?
quiz.q1.speaker: interviewer

lines.quiz.q1-why: A few very slow requests pull the average up. The distribution has a long tail, so report percentiles.

quiz.q2.caption: What does "p99 is 2 seconds" mean?
quiz.q2.voice: What does p99 is two seconds mean?
quiz.q2.speaker: interviewer

lines.quiz.q2-why: Ninety-nine in a hundred requests take two seconds or less. One in a hundred takes longer.

quiz.q3.caption: A page calls 10 services in parallel, each slow 1% of the time. Roughly how often is the page slow?
quiz.q3.voice: A page calls ten services in parallel, each slow one percent of the time. Roughly how often is the page slow?
quiz.q3.speaker: interviewer

lines.quiz.q3-why: It waits for the slowest call: one minus point nine nine to the tenth power, about ten percent.

quiz.q4.caption: A server goes from 80% to 95% busy. What happens to response time?
quiz.q4.voice: A server goes from eighty percent to ninety-five percent busy. What happens to response time?
quiz.q4.speaker: interviewer

lines.quiz.q4-why: Queues grow steeply near full capacity. In the simple queueing model it goes from five times the service time to twenty: four times worse.

quiz.retry.caption: {right} / 4. Worth another pass.
quiz.retry.voice: Not quite there. Replay a chapter or two, then try again.

lines.keywords.1: Before we wrap up, here are the words worth keeping.
lines.keywords.ask: Flip each card. Star the ones you want to practise later.
lines.keywords.hint: Tap a card to flip it. Press Done when you're ready.
lines.keywords.done: Starred words go to your flashcards. A few minutes a day keeps them fresh.
lines.finish.1: That's the lesson, and level one. Measure percentiles, not averages, watch the tail as calls fan out, and leave headroom before the queue explodes.
lines.finish.2: Next up: how a database actually reads those rows from disk.
